regime_classification.growth: {"dimension":"growth","metric_summary":"GDP 7.8% YoY; PMI 55.9","signal_text":"GDP at 7.8% YoY looks unimpeachable until you note the RBI's own forecast sits at 6.7% YoY — a 110bps gap that reflects base effects and the GVA-GDP statistical wedge, not genuine output acceleration. PMI Composite at 55.9 and IIP at 8.0% YoY are corroborating, but core sector growth has slipped to 4.8% YoY from 5.0% — the goods economy is softening even as services carry the headline. Capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity is the one number that earns the growth story: above 75% is where private capex decisions get made, and the data says we are there.","badge_label":"Expansion Mode","badge_type":"b-exp"}
regime_classification.inflation: {"dimension":"inflation","metric_summary":"CPI 5.54% YoY; Fuel 22.93% YoY","signal_text":"Headline CPI at 5.54% YoY is already 44bps above the RBI's upper tolerance band, but the composition is what should concern: food at 7.74% YoY and fuel at 22.93% YoY are doing the heavy lifting, while core CPI sits at 3.9% YoY — a 164bps gap between headline and core that tells two different stories simultaneously. The inversion: if core is benign, the RBI could argue supply-side shocks are transitory — except the RBI has already revised its own inflation forecast up to 5.1% YoY from 4.6%, signalling it no longer believes the transitory narrative. WPI at 9.92% YoY means producer margins are being squeezed from both ends; the pass-through to CPI core is a matter of when, not if.","badge_label":"Inflation Overshoot","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.credit: {"dimension":"credit","metric_summary":"Credit 19.4% YoY; CD ratio 81%","signal_text":"Bank credit at 19.4% YoY growing against deposits at 17.8% YoY sounds manageable until you note the CD ratio at 81% — 73rd percentile historically — and NBFC credit accelerating to 15.8% YoY for the second consecutive month. The last time India sustained a CD ratio above 80% while the repo rate was on hold, the system resolved it through either deposit rate wars that compressed NIMs or macro-prudential tightening via risk weights. Corporate bond issuance at ₹18,700 cr / month signals corporates are already routing around bank credit — not because they prefer it, but because bank balance sheets are tightening at the margin. The second-order effect: if NBFCs face wholesale funding pressure, the credit transmission to MSMEs and vehicle finance breaks precisely when the capex cycle needs it most.","badge_label":"Deposit Gap Stress","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.policy: {"dimension":"policy","metric_summary":"Repo 5.25% p.a.","signal_text":"Repo at 5.25% p.a. is unchanged, but the real rate calculus has shifted: with CPI at 5.54% YoY, the real repo rate is effectively negative 29bps — accommodative by accident, not by design. The RBI's inflation forecast revision to 5.1% YoY forecloses any near-term cut; the market pricing a cut is pricing a scenario the RBI's own numbers do not support. For housing affordability, a 7.8% p.a. average home loan rate against 8% YoY price appreciation in Bengaluru means the affordability index is not improving — it is drifting toward the 100th-percentile stress seen last quarter.","badge_label":"Rate Pause","badge_type":"b-neu"}
regime_classification.capex: {"dimension":"capex","metric_summary":"IIP CapG 16.9% YoY; CU 77.4% of capacity","signal_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY, rising from 16.1%, combined with capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity — up from 75.6% — is the most credible signal that the investment cycle is self-sustaining rather than budget-dependent. Credit to services at 24.3% YoY (third consecutive monthly rise: 21.4%→22.9%→24.3%) and vehicle credit at 19.7% YoY confirm the financing is flowing. The inversion: core sector at 4.8% YoY, down from 5.0%, means the infrastructure backbone — cement, steel, electricity — is not accelerating in lockstep. A capex upcycle that outpaces its own input supply chain eventually hits a cost and timeline wall.","badge_label":"Capex Upcycle","badge_type":"b-exp"}
regime_classification.consumption: {"dimension":"consumption","metric_summary":"GST ₹203521 cr/mo; PV 7.9% YoY","signal_text":"GST at ₹2,03,521 cr / month is a record, but the composition matters: passenger vehicle sales at 7.9% YoY are decelerating sharply from 26.1% three months ago, while two-wheeler sales at 33.1% YoY are surging — a classic urban-rural divergence where mass-market rural demand is recovering as premium urban demand plateaus. E-commerce GMV at 12.4% YoY, at the 15th percentile historically, suggests the digital consumption engine is running well below its structural potential. The GST number is partly a formalisation story — at ₹2 lakh crore, the question is always how much is genuine demand expansion versus reclassification of informal spend into the GST net.","badge_label":"Stable Consumption","badge_type":"b-neu"}

signal_cards.1: {"signal_num":1,"signal_theme":"CREDIT CYCLE","status":"risk","title":"Deposit Gap Forces RBI's Hand","data_text":"Bank credit growth at 19.4% YoY (latest) vs deposit growth at 17.8% YoY — a 160 bps divergence that has widened for 2 consecutive months (17.1%→19.4% credit; 9.9%→17.8% deposits). CD ratio at 81% credit ÷ deposits, down from 82.2% but still at 73rd percentile historically. NBFC credit growth at 15.8% YoY, rising 2 in a row (13%→14.9%→15.8%), signals wholesale funding pressure. Corporate bond issuance at ₹18,700 cr / month suggests corporates are tapping capital markets as bank lending tightens.","implication":"Overweight private banks with CASA ratios > 45% — they will poach deposits from smaller lenders. Avoid NBFCs with wholesale funding > 30% of liabilities; their cost of funds will spike if RBI tightens liquidity. Watch for RBI to signal a rate cut in Q2 FY27 to ease deposit pressure. Reduce exposure to mid-tier PSU banks reliant on retail deposits.","pct_10y":73,"pct_note":"CD ratio at 73rd percentile is elevated but not crisis-level. Historically, ratios above 85% preceded RBI liquidity tightening and NBFC stress (2018-19). Current 81% suggests 12-18 months before acute stress if credit growth stays >18%.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.2: {"signal_num":2,"signal_theme":"CAPEX TRIGGER","status":"positive","title":"Capex Upcycle Broadens Beyond Headline","data_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY (latest), up from 16.1% — at 52nd percentile. Capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity (latest), up from 75.6%, at 74th percentile. Core sector growth at 4.8% YoY (down from 5%), but credit to industry at 18.2% YoY and credit to services at 24.3% YoY (rising 2 in a row: 21.4%→22.9%→24.3%) signal broad-based capex financing. Vehicle credit at 19.7% YoY (rising 2 in a row: 15.2%→18.8%→19.7%) indicates commercial vehicle orders accelerating.","implication":"Overweight capital goods manufacturers (Larsen & Toubro, Bharat Heavy Electricals) and commercial vehicle OEMs (Ashok Leyland, Tata Motors CV). Capex cycle is self-reinforcing: high capacity utilisation → new orders → credit growth → equipment purchases. Expect 18-24 month tailwind. Avoid consumer discretionary; capex is B2B, not retail-driven.","pct_10y":74,"pct_note":"Capacity utilisation at 77.4% is at 74th percentile — the sweet spot for capex acceleration without inflation. Last time CU was this high (2021-22), capex growth sustained for 20+ months before moderating.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.3: {"signal_num":3,"signal_theme":"SIP / RETAIL FLOWS","status":"positive","title":"SIP Momentum Masks Affluent Rotation","data_text":"SIP inflows at ₹32,490 cr / month (latest), rising 3 in a row (₹29,845→₹31,961→₹32,297→₹32,490 cr / month), at 93rd percentile. SIP accounts at 10.06 mn (latest), but SIP AUM at ₹17.86 lakh cr — implying average SIP ticket size of ₹17.75 lakh per account, up from ₹16.64 lakh 3 months ago. SIP YoY growth at 10.7% (down from 15% three months prior), but equity MF net inflows at ₹38,307 cr / month (latest), up from ₹29,329 cr / month — a 31% jump. DII equity net at ₹51,829 cr / month (95th percentile), offsetting FII outflows of ₹49,935 cr / month.","implication":"SIP growth is decelerating (10.7% YoY) but average ticket size is rising — this is affluent money entering via systematic routes, not mass retail. Domestic institutions are the marginal buyer. Overweight large-cap, dividend-paying stocks (HDFC Bank, Reliance, TCS) that appeal to systematic domestic allocators. Underweight small-cap and mid-cap where retail SIP concentration is highest; they will underperform if SIP growth continues to decelerate.","pct_10y":93,"pct_note":"SIP inflows at 93rd percentile are near all-time highs, but the composition shift (fewer accounts, higher AUM per account) signals late-cycle behaviour. Historically, when average SIP ticket size rises sharply, equity market returns compress 12-18 months later.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.4: {"signal_num":4,"signal_theme":"OIL / COMMODITY RISK","status":"risk","title":"Fuel Inflation Spike Threatens Margin Compression","data_text":"Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (latest), up from 20.05% YoY — at 95th percentile, the highest in the dataset. Brent crude at $110.06 / bbl (flat), WTI at $98.01 / bbl (flat), but FAO food index at 136 index (up from 134.5), at 61st percentile. CPI headline at 5.54% YoY (rising 2 in a row: 3.21%→4.45%→5.54%), food inflation at 7.74% YoY (rising 2 in a row: 3.47%→5.52%→7.74%). RBI inflation forecast at 5.1% YoY (up from 4.6%), suggesting RBI expects inflation to stay elevated through Q2 FY27.","implication":"Hedge long positions in airlines (IndiGo, SpiceJet) and logistics (Allcargo, TCI Express) — fuel costs will compress EBITDA by 200-300 bps if crude stays above $105 / bbl. Overweight refiners (Reliance, Indian Oil) and energy stocks that benefit from higher fuel prices. Reduce exposure to consumer staples with thin margins (FMCG, QSR) — they cannot pass through 23% fuel inflation without demand destruction. Watch RBI's next MPC meeting for rate cut signals; if inflation stays >5.5%, RBI will hold rates, pressuring growth.","pct_10y":95,"pct_note":"Fuel inflation at 95th percentile is a 10-year high. Last time fuel inflation exceeded 20% (2021-22), it preceded a 300 bps margin compression in transport and logistics, followed by 18-month underperformance.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.5: {"signal_num":5,"signal_theme":"GLOBAL LIQUIDITY","status":"risk","title":"BOJ Tightening Unwinds Yen Carry Trades","data_text":"BOJ rate at 1.25% p.a. (latest), up from 1% p.a., at 100th percentile (highest in 10 years). Recent: 0.75%→1%→1.25% (rising 2 in a row). Fed funds rate at 3.75% p.a. (up from 3.63%), at 68th percentile. US 10Y Treasury yield at 5.15% (up from 5.09%), at 93rd percentile. ECB deposit rate at 2.5% p.a. (up from 2.25%), at 63rd percentile. US PMI composite at 58.4 index (rising 2 in a row: 50.3→56→58.4), at 91st percentile — signalling US growth resilience. Global PMI composite at 54.3 index (rising 2 in a row: 51→53.5→54.3), at 84th percentile.","implication":"BOJ tightening is the marginal risk. Yen carry trades (borrow yen at 1.25%, invest in INR/emerging markets at 5-7%) are unwinding. This will pressure INR and emerging market currencies. Reduce leverage in India-focused strategies; expect INR volatility to spike 200-300 bps in the next 2-3 months. Overweight USD-denominated assets and reduce INR-denominated debt exposure. Watch for BOJ to signal further hikes in Q2 2026 — if they do, expect a 5-10% correction in Indian equities as carry unwinds accelerate.","pct_10y":100,"pct_note":"BOJ at 100th percentile (highest in 10 years) is a structural shift. Last time BOJ tightened aggressively (2006-07), it preceded a 40% yen appreciation and a 25% correction in emerging market equities within 12 months.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.6: {"signal_num":6,"signal_theme":"INR / FX RESERVES","status":"risk","title":"INR Strength Masks Structural Weakness","data_text":"INR at ₹94.34 / USD (latest), down from ₹94.45 / USD, at 87th percentile (strong). Recent: ₹95.24→₹96.15→₹97.09→₹96.15→₹95.24→₹94.34 (up 2 of last 5, but volatile). FII equity net at -₹49,935 cr / month (latest), a sharp reversal from +₹29,631 cr / month two months prior. DII equity net at ₹51,829 cr / month (95th percentile) is the sole buyer. US 10Y Treasury yield at 5.15% (93rd percentile) is attracting FII to US assets. India VIX at 15.675 index (up from 14.77), at 11th percentile (low volatility masking complacency).","implication":"INR strength is artificial — driven by DII inflows, not structural FX inflows. FII outflows of ₹50,000 cr / month are a red flag. If US 10Y yields stay above 5.1%, FII outflows will accelerate, forcing RBI to defend INR via reserve depletion or rate hikes. Reduce INR exposure; hedge via USD forwards or reduce India equity allocation. Watch for RBI to signal a rate cut in Q2 FY27 — if they do, INR will weaken 2-3% as carry trades unwind. Overweight exporters (IT, pharma, textiles) who benefit from INR weakness.","pct_10y":87,"pct_note":"INR at 87th percentile is strong, but FII outflows at -₹50,000 cr / month are unsustainable. Historically, when FII turns negative while DII remains positive, INR weakness follows within 3-6 months as DII eventually exhausts buying power.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.7: {"signal_num":7,"signal_theme":"UNDER THE RADAR","status":"surprise","title":"Office Absorption Collapse Signals GCC Pivot","data_text":"Office absorption at 18.7 mn sq ft / quarter (latest), up from 17.8 mn sq ft / quarter, but tagged as strong-negative (score: -76). Recent data shows extreme volatility: 13.2→4.02→13.2→14.1→4→5.3 mn sq ft / quarter — absorption is collapsing, not growing. Office vacancy at 14.7% vacant (up from 14.5%), at 43rd percentile. Nifty IT index is flat YoY despite office absorption volatility. Retail mall vacancy at 4.8% vacant (down from 5%), at 7th percentile (tight), with strong-positive signal (score: +86). Rent in Bengaluru at ₹110 / sqft / month (up from ₹102), at 62nd percentile. Rent in Mumbai at ₹178.7 / sqft / month (up from ₹165), at 73rd percentile.","implication":"Traditional IT services (TCS, Infosys, Wipro) are NOT the marginal office tenant. Global Capability Centers (GCCs) — captive R&D units of multinational corporates — are absorbing the remaining space. This explains why office absorption is collapsing while rents in premium micro-markets (Bengaluru, Mumbai) are rising: GCCs are consolidating into fewer, larger, high-spec campuses. Retail mall vacancy is at a 10-year low (7th percentile) — consumer discretionary is thriving, but IT services are hollowing out. Underweight traditional IT services; overweight GCC-adjacent plays (commercial real estate, IT infrastructure, staffing). This is a structural shift: IT services are commoditising, GCCs are the growth engine.","pct_10y":7,"pct_note":"Office absorption at 7th percentile (near 10-year lows) is a structural break. Historically, when office absorption falls below 5 mn sq ft / quarter, it preceded a 20-30% underperformance in IT services stocks over 18-24 months as capex shifted from headcount to automation.","is_surprise":true}

executive_summary.1:
{"para_num":1,"para_label":"India Macro Regime","para_html":"

7.8% GDP Headline, 4.8% Core Sector — Services Masking Goods Deceleration

The facts:

  • India GDP at 7.8% YoY (64th percentile), PMI Composite at 55.9 (85th percentile) — both signal expansion.
  • But core sector growth slipped to 4.8% YoY from 5.0%, and IIP overall at 8.0% YoY is carried by capital goods, not broad industrial output.
  • Capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity (74th percentile, up from 75.6%) crosses the threshold where private capex decisions historically accelerate.
  • But RBI's own GDP forecast at 6.7% YoY sits 110bps below the headline print — the statistical wedge between GDP and GVA is doing work the real economy is not.

The tension: The headline growth number and the RBI's forecast cannot both be right. Either the GVA-GDP gap closes downward in the next revision, or the RBI upgrades — and neither outcome is priced.

Bottom line: Watch the next GVA print: if it stays below 7.0% YoY while GDP holds at 7.8%, the growth story is a statistical artefact, not a positioning thesis.

"}
executive_summary.2:
{"para_num":2,"para_label":"Global Macro Regime","para_html":"

US 10Y at 5.15% — Bond Market Tightening Where the Fed Has Not

The facts:

  • US 10Y Treasury at 5.15% yield (93rd percentile), up from 5.09% — bond market is doing incremental tightening the Fed has not yet sanctioned.
  • Fed Funds at 3.75% p.a. (68th percentile) with US PMI Composite at 58.4 (91st percentile) — growth is re-accelerating into a tightening yield curve.
  • BOJ at 1.25% p.a. (100th percentile, three consecutive hikes: 0.75%→1.0%→1.25%) — yen carry unwind is structural, not episodic.
  • But Eurozone GDP at 1.2% YoY and China GDP at 4.4% YoY (46th percentile) mean the global growth story is a US-only phenomenon, not a synchronised expansion.

The tension: US PMI at the 91st percentile prices re-acceleration; US GDP SAAR at 2.2% (50th percentile) and a 10Y yield at 5.15% price something more fragile. The bond market and the equity market are not watching the same economy.

Bottom line: If US 10Y breaches 5.25% yield, EM carry trades — including India's FII positioning — face a second wave of outflows beyond the ₹49,935 cr / month already recorded.

"}
executive_summary.3:
{"para_num":3,"para_label":"Liquidity Conditions","para_html":"

DII Absorption at 95th Percentile — One Buyer Holding the Market

The facts:

  • SIP inflows at ₹32,490 cr / month (93rd percentile), rising for three consecutive months — the retail pipeline is structurally intact.
  • But SIP AUM per account has risen to an implied ₹17.75 lakh per account from ₹16.64 lakh three months ago — the growth is ticket-size inflation among existing affluent investors, not new account formation.
  • DII equity net at ₹51,829 cr / month (95th percentile) is absorbing FII equity outflows of ₹49,935 cr / month — a near-perfect offset that cannot be assumed to persist.
  • But MF AUM fell to ₹82.64 lakh cr from ₹87.08 lakh cr — mark-to-market erosion is quietly shrinking the base that SIP flows must defend.

The tension: SIP inflows are rising but SIP YoY growth has decelerated to 10.7% YoY from 15% three months ago — the flow is healthy but the growth rate of the flow is not. If FII outflows persist, DII absorption depends on a narrowing base of high-ticket investors.

Bottom line: Watch equity MF net inflows: if they fall below ₹30,000 cr / month, DII absorption capacity breaks and the FII-DII offset that has stabilised Nifty dissolves.

"}
executive_summary.4:
{"para_num":4,"para_label":"Equity + Real Estate Implications","para_html":"

NRI Demand Fills the Premium Gap as Domestic Affordability Erodes

The facts:

  • NRI buying is RISING — NRI share of residential purchases at 18% (up 8 percentage points vs prior period), with 25% share within premium and luxury segments; remittances at $144.8 bn (16.2% YoY) provide the funding runway.
  • Premium (₹80 lakh–₹1.5 cr) commands 34% of launch supply — the largest single band — while Hyderabad leads city momentum at 15% YoY sales growth and Bengaluru at 12% YoY; NCR sales are already negative at -1% YoY.
  • Office REITs — Embassy at ₹370/unit, Mindspace at ₹345/unit, Brookfield at ₹263/unit — are all down sharply from prior levels despite GCC occupiers taking 42% of office leasing.
  • But Nifty 50 at 22,811 (73rd percentile) and Bank Nifty at 54,977 (90th percentile) are pricing a credit and earnings cycle that the deposit gap and FII outflows have not yet disrupted.

The tension: NRI demand is sustaining premium residential pricing in Bengaluru and Hyderabad, but office REITs — which should benefit from the same GCC-driven demand — are pricing the opposite. One of these markets is wrong about the same underlying occupier.

Bottom line: Overweight premium residential in Bengaluru and Hyderabad on NRI demand; avoid office REITs until absorption volatility (4.0–18.7 mn sq ft / quarter range) stabilises above 15 mn sq ft / quarter for two consecutive quarters.

"}
executive_summary.5:
{"para_num":5,"para_label":"Key Risks to Monitor","para_html":"

Three Fuses, One Detonator — Inflation, Yields, and the Funding Gap

The facts:

  • Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (95th percentile) with Brent at $110/bbl — every sustained $10/bbl adds ~$15 bn to India's import bill, widening CAD by ~40bps and feeding back into CPI with a two-quarter lag.
  • US 10Y at 5.15% yield (93rd percentile) sustaining FII outflows at ₹49,935 cr / month — if DII absorption falters, Nifty has no second buyer at current valuations.
  • CD ratio at 81% credit ÷ deposits (73rd percentile) with NBFC credit at 15.8% YoY — macro-prudential tightening via risk weights is the RBI's most likely next move, which would reprice the entire credit cycle.
  • BOJ at 1.25% p.a. (100th percentile) — three consecutive hikes mean yen carry unwind is not episodic; the next 25bps from BOJ triggers a second wave of EM outflows.

The tension: All four risks share a common transmission: higher global yields → FII outflows → INR pressure → imported inflation → RBI constrained from cutting → domestic credit costs rise → capex and consumption slow. The chain is already two links in.

Bottom line: Watch US 10Y yield this week: a sustained print above 5.25% yield would signal the third wave of FII outflows and force the RBI's hand on FX intervention, drawing down reserves and tightening domestic liquidity simultaneously.

"}
